summary.text: Boyle's law says that for a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional.
In practice, when the volume is halved the pressure doubles, and when the volume is doubled the pressure is halved.
It is named after Robert Boyle, who published the original law in 1662 after experiments in which he squeezed air in a closed J-shaped tube.

facts.label: Landmark
facts.value: Law expressed as an equation linking two variable quantities

facts.label: Apparatus
facts.value: Built by Robert Hooke, according to some authorities

items.prompt: You seal a syringe of gas at steady temperature and push the plunger to half its original volume. What happens to the gas pressure?

options.label: It stays the same
It halves
It quadruples
It doubles

items.explain: When the volume is halved, the pressure is doubled, as long as the temperature and amount of gas are unchanged.

items.prompt: A gas is heated while it is squeezed. Why can Boyle's law alone not predict the result?

options.label: It only works for gases that are not squeezed
It only holds when temperature and amount of gas stay unchanged
It only works for liquids that are heated
It only applies to air inside a J-shaped tube

items.explain: The pressure-volume relationship holds if the temperature and amount of gas stay unchanged in a closed system.

items.prompt: A gas at pressure 2 fills volume 6. At the same temperature its volume is squeezed to 3. What is the new pressure?
items.explain: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ gives 2 × 6 = P₂ × 3, so P₂ is 4.

items.prompt: Why does squeezing a trapped gas make it take up less room?

options.label: Its particles shrink under the force
Its particles escape through the container
Its particles are forced closer together
Its particles lose their motion entirely

items.explain: As the pressure on a gas increases, its volume decreases because the gas particles are forced closer together.

items.prompt: Some books give this law a double-barrelled name. What is behind that?

options.label: Two scientists wrote up their experiments together
A French physicist found the same law on his own, later
One scientist fixed the other's equation
A mistake in an old textbook merged two laws

items.explain: Edme Mariotte discovered the same law independently of Boyle in 1679, so it is sometimes called the Boyle–Mariotte law.

items.prompt: Boyle's measurements fit the law neatly. What helps explain why no deviations showed up then?

options.label: The era's equipment could not reach very high pressures or very low temperatures
Real gases follow the law perfectly at every pressure
Boyle only ever tested gases that were not air
Early experimenters kept the temperature changing

items.explain: 17th-century technology could not produce very high pressures or very low temperatures, so deviations were unlikely; later improvements made them noticeable.
